chapter.title: What it owes: debts, soon and later

cards.body: Open the kitchen drawer in the house. Inside: the electricity bill due Friday, the plumber's invoice, this month's card statement. On the shelf above sits the mortgage folder, 22 years still to run. All of it is money owed, but **only the drawer needs paying this year**. A balance sheet keeps the same two piles.
cards.simpler: Picture a kitchen drawer at home. Inside are the bills you must pay soon: the electricity bill due Friday, the plumber's invoice, this month's card statement. On the shelf above sits the mortgage folder, with 22 years left to run. All of it is money owed. But **only the drawer needs paying this year**. A company's balance sheet, the list of what it owns and owes, keeps those same two piles apart.

cards.prompt: Maya's bakery owes three things: 4,000 to the flour supplier, due in 30 days; a 60,000 bank loan repaid over 8 years; and 1,200 in tax due next quarter. Which one belongs on the shelf, not in the drawer?

whyNot.a: That's a drawer item, not a shelf item: 30 days is well inside the next 12 months.
whyNot.c: That's a drawer item too: next quarter arrives within 12 months.

cards.reteach: The split is one question: must this be paid within the next 12 months? The supplier and the tax office both want money inside a year. The bank loan stretches over 8 years, so most of it sits on the shelf.

cards.title: The 12-month line
cards.body:
*Liabilities* is the sheet's word for everything the company owes. It sorts them with one question: **is it due within 12 months?**

If yes, it is a *current liability*. The usual names are *trade payables* or *accounts payable* (bills from suppliers), *short-term borrowings* (loans due this year), *taxes payable*, and *accrued expenses* (costs already run up but not yet billed, like last week's wages).

If it is due later than 12 months, it is a *non-current* or *long-term liability*: long-term borrowings, bonds, and lease liabilities for buildings or vans rented for years.
cards.simpler: Liabilities is the word the balance sheet uses for everything the company owes. It sorts them with one question: **is it due within 12 months?** If yes, it is a current liability. Common ones are bills from suppliers (trade payables or accounts payable), loans due this year, taxes owed, and costs already run up but not yet billed, like last week's wages. If it is due later than 12 months, it is a non-current or long-term liability, such as long bank loans, bonds, or multi-year leases on buildings or vans.

cards.title: Pinewood Furniture's drawer
cards.body: Pinewood Furniture, a made-up firm, lists trade payables of 310,000 to its wood and fabric suppliers, short-term borrowings of 150,000, and taxes payable of 40,000. Current liabilities total 500,000. Below that, a bank loan of 900,000, due in 2031. Someone skimming says "they owe 1.4 million" and goes pale. But the question for this year is 500,000. The 900,000 is the mortgage folder: real, but not knocking on the door yet.
cards.simpler: Pinewood Furniture is a made-up company. It owes 310,000 to its wood and fabric suppliers, 150,000 in short-term loans, and 40,000 in taxes. Those are the current liabilities, and they add up to 500,000. Below sits a bank loan of 900,000, not due until 2031. Someone skimming says "they owe 1.4 million" and panics. But the question for this year is 500,000. The 900,000 is the mortgage folder: **real, but not knocking on the door yet**.

cards.prompt: A delivery company's sheet shows two lines: "Lease liabilities (non-current) 2,400,000" and "Lease liabilities (current) 300,000". You are writing down what it must pay in the next 12 months. Which goes on your list?

whyNot.a: That's the shelf, not the drawer: non-current means due after 12 months.
whyNot.c: That's the full lease, not this year's share: only the current part is due within 12 months.

cards.reteach: One long lease gets cut into two lines. The slice due this year is labelled current. The rest is labelled non-current and waits on the shelf. Your 12-month list only takes the current slice.

cards.title: One loan, two lines
cards.body:
The example hides a trick worth knowing. A 10-year loan does not sit entirely on the shelf. This year's repayments are moved down into current liabilities, often as a line called *current portion of long-term debt*. **The same loan appears twice**, split by due date. Don't add it up twice, and don't miss the slice in the drawer.

Each line also tells you who is owed. Payables are suppliers. Borrowings are banks or bondholders. Taxes payable is the government. Accrued wages are staff. *Deferred revenue* is customers who paid early for something not yet delivered, like a year's gym membership. The footnotes give the exact due dates when you need them.
cards.simpler: There is a trick here. A 10-year loan does not sit entirely on the shelf. This year's repayments get moved down into current liabilities, usually under a line called current portion of long-term debt. So **the same loan appears twice**, split by when it is due. Don't count it twice, and don't miss the slice in the drawer. Each line also tells you who is owed: suppliers, banks, the government, staff, or customers who paid early for something not yet delivered, like a year's gym pass.

cards.body: Dev adds up every liability line, gets 1.4 million, sees cash of 200,000, and announces the company is sunk. He never asked the one question: due when? The 900,000 loan is paid over 8 years. Spot this mistake whenever someone quotes total liabilities as if it were all due tomorrow.
cards.simpler: Dev adds up every liability line and gets 1.4 million. He sees cash of 200,000 and announces the company is finished. He never asked the one question: **due when?** The 900,000 loan gets paid back over 8 years, not this month. It is like saying someone with a mortgage is broke because they cannot pay the whole house off today. Watch for this mistake whenever someone quotes total liabilities as if all of it were due tomorrow.

cards.prompt: Which of these is a current liability?

options.text: A bond that is repaid in full in 2039
Wages staff earned last week, paid next Friday
The non-current part of a 6-year van lease

whyNot.a: That's long-term debt, not current: 2039 is years past the 12-month line.
whyNot.c: That's the shelf part of the lease, not the drawer part: the label non-current says it is due after 12 months.

cards.reteach: Current means due within 12 months, whoever is owed. Wages owed from last week are an accrued expense and get paid in days. A bond due in 2039 and the non-current part of a lease both wait past the 12-month line.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Liabilities are what the company owes, split by one question: **due within 12 months or later?** The current pile is the drawer it must empty this year; the non-current pile is the mortgage on the shelf, and a long loan shows up in both.
cards.simpler: Liabilities are what the company owes. They are split by one question: **due within 12 months or later?** The current pile is the kitchen drawer, the bills the company must clear this year. The non-current pile is the mortgage folder on the shelf, real but not due yet. One long loan can show up in both piles, with this year's slice in the drawer and the rest on the shelf.

cards.body: Open any annual report you can find online, search for "Total current liabilities" and "Total non-current liabilities", and write the two numbers side by side. Note which one is bigger.
cards.simpler: Find any company's annual report online. Search the balance sheet for two lines: "Total current liabilities" and "Total non-current liabilities". Write the two numbers side by side on a piece of paper. Then note which one is bigger. That is the drawer next to the mortgage folder, and **the split tells you more than the total ever will**. It takes about five minutes and makes the idea stick.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now list what a company must pay in the next 12 months, what can wait, and who is owed each amount.
